summary: Gives guidance on securing manually configured IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnels using IPsec in transport mode. No new protocol extensions are described, only how to use the existing IPsec framework. It is informational.

eli5.summary: If you send IPv6 packets through an IPv4 tunnel, anyone could peek into the tunnel. This note shows how to lock it using tools that already exist.

questions: how to secure ipv6 in ipv4 tunnels
what is transport mode vs tunnel mode for ipsec
how do i set up ike for tunnel endpoints
subtitle: Protecting IPv6 traffic tunneled through IPv4 networks with IPsec.

tldr.problem: IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnels allow nodes to tunnel IPv6 traffic over IPv4 networks, but the unencrypted tunnels are vulnerable to address spoofing and eavesdropping.
tldr.mechanism: IPsec in transport mode can protect the tunnel by encrypting and authenticating IPv6 packets as they traverse the IPv4 network, and IKE handles automated key exchange.
tldr.outcome: The RFC recommends transport mode as the simplest and most practical way to secure manually configured IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnels without requiring IPv6 prefix knowledge a priori.

today: RFC 4891 remains the authoritative guidance for securing manually configured IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnels with IPsec. As IPv6 deployment has matured, these tunnels are less common, but the document provides essential security guidance for legacy and transition deployments.

sections.title: Introduction and Threat Model
sections.content:
IPv6-in-IPv4 tunneling, standardized in RFC 4213, is an IPv6 transition mechanism that lets routers and hosts tunnel IPv6 packets across IPv4 networks by encapsulating them in IPv4 packets. This document addresses security risks in manually configured tunnels.

The main threats are address spoofing: an attacker can spoof the outer IPv4 source address of the encapsulating packet, or spoof the inner IPv6 source address of the encapsulated packet. Unlike the IPv4 Internet, where address spoofing is mitigated by ingress filtering at network edges, IPv6 packets escaping the tunnel may bypass IPv6 ingress filtering. IPsec provides stronger protection by ensuring that packets come from the authenticated tunnel peer and have not been modified in transit.
sections.eli5: When an IPv6 packet travels inside an IPv4 tunnel, two things could go wrong: someone could pretend to send the outer packet from the wrong place, or someone could pretend the inner packet came from a different IPv6 address. IPsec stops both tricks.

sections.title: IPsec Transport vs Tunnel Mode
sections.content:
IPsec offers two modes for protecting tunnel traffic. Transport mode protects the payload while preserving the outer IPv4 header, allowing the existing tunnel mechanism to operate unchanged. The IPsec transform is applied to traffic identified by (IPv4-source, IPv4-destination, protocol = 41), which represents IPv6 packets in IPv4. A successful IPsec verification proves the packet came from the correct IPv4 tunnel endpoint.

Tunnel mode protects both the outer IPv4 header and the entire inner packet by creating an IPsec tunnel, but it requires knowing IPv6 prefixes in advance for proper security policy configuration. In many implementations, tunnel mode cannot protect all necessary traffic (link-local, multicast) without explicit prefix knowledge. The RFC recommends transport mode because it is simpler to implement and deploy, especially when IPv6 source addresses cannot be predicted a priori.
sections.eli5: Transport mode is like putting a seal on an envelope while still showing the address. Tunnel mode is like putting the whole envelope inside a lockbox. For these tunnels, transport mode works better because you don't need to know all the addresses ahead of time.

sections.title: Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC describes three main scenarios. Router-to-router tunnels connect two IPv6 routers across an IPv4 infrastructure. Source and destination IPv6 addresses can come from any prefix learned through routing, so binding specific addresses to the security policy is not feasible. IPv6 ingress filtering on the tunnel interface must mitigate inner address spoofing.

Site-to-router or router-to-site tunnels connect a site's border router to an upstream provider's router, or a single host to an intermediary router. The site originates packets with known IPv6 prefixes, allowing verification that packets come from the expected prefix.

Host-to-host tunnels span the entire end-to-end path between two IPv6 hosts. The source and destination IPv6 addresses are known a priori, making it possible to bind them directly to the security policy and prevent IPv6 source address spoofing completely.
sections.eli5: Tunnels work differently depending on what is on each end. If two routers talk to the whole internet, you can't check every address. If a site talks to just one router, you can verify the site's addresses. If two hosts talk to each other, you can lock down exactly which addresses are allowed.

sections.title: Configuration and Key Management
sections.content:
For transport mode, the Security Policy Database (SPD) must include rules to protect IPv6 traffic (protocol 41) between the tunnel endpoints, while allowing IKE and ESP traffic to bypass IPsec processing. The packet format consists of an IPv4 header with tunnel endpoint addresses, an ESP header for protection, the IPv6 header and payload inside.

Key management must use either IKEv1 or IKEv2 for automated security association establishment; manual keying is strongly discouraged because large amounts of IPv6 traffic traversing the tunnel make key recovery easier for attackers. IKEv2 is preferred where supported, as it includes useful features like support for dynamic address configuration via EAP methods and integrated NAT traversal. Peer authorization requires manual configuration of identity types and authentication methods, with IPv4 addresses of tunnel endpoints as the primary identity.
sections.eli5: You set up a list of rules saying 'protect all IPv6 traffic between these two addresses.' Then you run IKE, an automatic system, to create secret keys. You never type the keys in manually, or attackers could figure them out by watching lots of traffic.

sections.title: Summary and Best Practices
sections.content:
The RFC recommends applying IPsec transport mode to tunnel interfaces as the simplest and most practical solution for securing IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnels. Source address spoofing can be further limited by enabling IPv6 ingress filtering on the tunnel interface. IKEv2 should be used for key exchange where available; IKEv1 is acceptable as a fallback.

Tunnel mode is mentioned only for special cases where the tunnel endpoints are dynamic (such as mobile scenarios requiring MOBIKE support), but it is not recommended for general deployments due to configuration complexity and feature limitations. The document also discusses optional features in appendices, including dynamic IPv6 address configuration, NAT traversal, and tunnel endpoint discovery mechanisms.
sections.eli5: Use transport mode on the tunnel interface if you can. Turn on filtering to stop spoofed addresses. Use IKEv2 if your system supports it. Tunnel mode is only for special cases where addresses change a lot.
